Mosquito Control in Miami-Dade & Broward: A Dual-County Insider’s Guide

If you live near the county line on US-1, manage a rental property in Hialeah, or own a canal-front home in Davie, you already know that mosquito pressure doesn’t stop at jurisdictional boundaries. Miami-Dade and Broward share the same subtropical climate, the same canal infrastructure, and the same species making life uncomfortable outdoors. Yet most available resources address one county or the other — never both under a single, practical framework.

This guide covers the full picture: the specific mosquito species active across both counties, how South Florida’s wet and dry seasons shape your treatment calendar, what free public services actually cover (and where they stop), how different property types require different approaches, and what to look for when hiring a private pest management company. The goal is to help you make informed decisions — not to sell you on the first option you find.

At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, we’ve been treating South Florida properties from our base in Homestead since the company’s founding. We serve Miami-Dade and Broward homeowners, property managers, and businesses. Our approach uses precision-based, low-exposure methods — targeted mosquito spray combined with insect growth regulators (IGRs), station-based Eco Premium service, breeding-site treatment, mosquito bait, misting options, and on-demand repellency programs — matched to individual property conditions rather than applied uniformly across every job.

This resource is for homeowners doing real research before spending money, property managers trying to protect a guest experience, and health-conscious families who want effective mosquito reduction without saturating their yard with chemical residue.

Why South Florida Mosquitoes Don’t Follow a “Season”

Most of the country thinks about mosquitoes the way they think about snow — a seasonal inconvenience that arrives, peaks, and goes away. South Florida doesn’t work that way.

Here’s the more accurate mental model: South Florida operates on a mosquito cycle driven by rainfall, not temperature. Because temperatures rarely drop below the threshold that slows mosquito development, the population never collapses the way it does in temperate climates. What changes is intensity, and that intensity tracks directly with water accumulation.

The South Florida Mosquito Calendar

Dry Season (roughly November through April): Mosquito populations drop to their lowest point, but they don’t disappear. Standing water sources dry up, reducing breeding sites, but established populations persist in shaded, moist microhabitats — dense bromeliads, irrigation-saturated landscaping, and covered containers that retain water. During this window, a single missed treatment won’t create an emergency, but it does allow populations to rebuild their baseline.

Wet Season (roughly May through October): This is where South Florida diverges sharply from anywhere else in the country. Afternoon thunderstorms deposit rainfall almost daily. Low-lying areas flood. Bromeliads fill to capacity. Pool covers accumulate standing water. The mosquito population can rebuild from near-zero to nuisance levels within seven to ten days of a rain event, because Aedes aegypti can complete its life cycle from egg to biting adult in roughly one week under South Florida summer conditions.

Hurricane and Tropical Storm Events: Storm surge and flooding create mass breeding events. After a significant tropical weather system, standing water persists in places that don’t normally hold water — depressions in lawns, clogged gutters, tarps, overturned debris. The two to three weeks following a named storm represent some of the highest mosquito pressure the region experiences all year. Treatment frequency should increase during and after these events, not hold steady.

Practical implication: Mosquito management in South Florida is not a summer project. A recurring program running through the wet season, with adjusted frequency around storm events, outperforms any single or occasional treatment. The cycle is predictable once you understand it.

Three Species You’re Actually Dealing With in Miami-Dade and Broward

Generic mosquito content talks about “mosquitoes” as if they’re interchangeable. They’re not. The three species responsible for most of the biting pressure and disease risk across Miami-Dade and Broward have distinct behaviors, breeding preferences, and peak activity windows — which directly affects how treatment should be structured.

Aedes aegypti — The Yellow Fever Mosquito

What it looks like: Small, dark body with distinctive white lyre-shaped markings on the thorax and banded legs.

Behavior: Strongly urban-adapted. This species thrives in and around human structures, preferring small, artificial containers — flower pot saucers, discarded bottle caps, clogged gutters, tire swings, and roof gutters. It doesn’t need a pond or a ditch. A plastic cup with a half-inch of rainwater is sufficient.

Biting pattern: Aggressive daytime biter, with peak activity in the two hours after sunrise and the two hours before sunset. Unlike many mosquito species, it doesn’t back off at midday.

Peak pressure: Wet season, May through October, with the highest trap counts typically in late summer. Miami-Dade County collected 64,570 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in a single year across its surveillance network, and 399,418 total using 308 traps, according to a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spatiotemporal mosquito dynamics in the county.

Disease vector status: Primary local vector for Dengue fever, Zika virus, and Chikungunya. These are not theoretical risks in South Florida — local transmission events have occurred in Miami-Dade in recent years.

Most effective treatment approaches: Source reduction (eliminating small containers), precision larvicide applications in ornamental water features, and targeted adult barrier sprays focused on vegetation where adults rest during the day.

Aedes albopictus — The Asian Tiger Mosquito

What it looks like: Similar size to Ae. aegypti with bold black and white striping and a single white median stripe down the thorax.

Behavior: Also container-breeding, but tolerates a wider range of breeding sites than Ae. aegypti, including natural containers like tree holes, bromeliads, and bamboo internodes. More aggressive outdoors and slightly more prevalent in suburban and semi-rural environments, including areas near Everglades buffer zones and canal-side landscaping.

Biting pattern: Primarily a daytime biter, often more aggressive than Ae. aegypti at mid-morning and late afternoon.

Peak pressure: Wet season, with presence extending later into fall than many species due to its cold tolerance relative to other subtropical mosquitoes.

Disease vector status: Secondary vector for Dengue and Chikungunya; competent vector for numerous other arboviruses.

Most effective treatment approaches: Bromeliad treatments are especially important for this species in South Florida landscapes. Barrier sprays targeting dense vegetation and perimeter plantings, combined with source reduction in natural containers.

Culex quinquefasciatus — The Southern House Mosquito

What it looks like: Medium-sized, dull brown, without the bold markings of Aedes species.

Behavior: Breeds in stagnant, nutrient-rich water — ditches, storm drains, neglected swimming pools, sewage-influenced water, and the canal system that runs throughout Miami-Dade and Broward. This is the species most associated with the region’s extensive drainage infrastructure.

Biting pattern: Primarily nocturnal, with peak activity from dusk through the night. If mosquitoes are ruining your evening on a screened patio, Culex is often responsible.

Peak pressure: Peaks in mid-to-late summer when stagnant water reaches maximum temperatures. Miami-Dade County collected 1,250,879 Culex quinquefasciatus mosquitoes, making it by far the most numerically dominant species in county surveillance data, with 187,316 collected alone — per the same 2026 PLOS ONE study.

Disease vector status: Primary local vector for West Nile Virus and St. Louis Encephalitis. It feeds on birds as a preferred host, then bridges to humans, which is how West Nile transmission cycles operate.

Most effective treatment approaches: Larviciding of standing water sources — catch basins, ornamental ponds, standing irrigation water — combined with adult barrier treatments timed for the evening hours when this species is active.

Mosquito-Borne Disease Risks in Miami-Dade and Broward

The disease context matters here because it shapes how seriously to treat mosquito control — particularly for families with young children, elderly residents, or immunocompromised household members.

Dengue Fever: Transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, Dengue has caused locally-acquired cases in South Florida. Symptoms range from flu-like illness to severe hemorrhagic fever in repeat infections. Florida’s dense urban environment and year-round Aedes populations make ongoing transmission risk real, not theoretical.

Zika Virus: Also transmitted by Aedes aegypti, Zika’s connection to birth defects (particularly microcephaly) made Miami-Dade one of the most closely watched counties in the country during an outbreak, when local transmission was confirmed in Wynwood and Miami Beach. For anyone who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy, Aedes control around the home is a direct health measure.

West Nile Virus: Circulated by Culex quinquefasciatus, West Nile remains present in Florida’s bird populations every year. Most human infections are mild or asymptomatic, but neuroinvasive disease is a risk for older adults. Florida Department of Health surveillance tracks West Nile activity statewide throughout the summer months.

Chikungunya and Eastern Equine Encephalitis (EEE): Less common but present in the region. EEE is rare but carries a high mortality rate when neuroinvasive disease develops; it’s transmitted by Culex species feeding on infected birds, then bridging to humans.

For current disease surveillance data and health advisories specific to Florida, the Florida Department of Health maintains active reporting at their state health office resources.

Free Public Mosquito Control vs. Private Service: A Decision Framework

Both Miami-Dade and Broward counties operate public mosquito control programs funded by tax revenue. Many residents don’t know these services exist or don’t know how to access them. Here’s what each covers — and where the gaps are.

Miami-Dade County Mosquito Control: What Residents Should Know

Miami-Dade County’s Mosquito Control Division conducts surveillance-based operations across the county, using trap data to identify areas with elevated population pressure and direct aerial and ground spraying accordingly. This is a public health infrastructure function — it’s not a personalized yard service.

Residents can file a service request through Miami-Dade 311 when they observe significant mosquito activity. The county prioritizes requests based on surveillance data, weather conditions, and public health risk levels. During a Dengue or West Nile outbreak investigation, response may be faster and more targeted to specific neighborhoods.

The limitation is exactly what you’d expect from a public infrastructure service: it covers public spaces, drainage systems, and roadsides. Your backyard, your canal-adjacent lawn, your ornamental pond, your bromeliad garden — none of that is in scope. The county will treat the ditch at the edge of your property; it won’t treat the birdbath in your side yard.

Broward County Mosquito Control: Same Framework, Different Coverage Map

Broward County’s program operates similarly, with ground and aerial equipment deployed based on surveillance trap counts and complaint data. The county covers unincorporated areas and public water bodies. Many Broward residents in incorporated municipalities (Fort Lauderdale, Miramar, Pembroke Pines) may fall under their city’s program rather than the county’s directly — worth confirming with your city’s public works department.

When to Move Beyond Public Services

Public mosquito control is a valuable layer of regional management. It’s not a substitute for property-level control. If you’re experiencing mosquito pressure in your own yard, on your pool deck, or during outdoor gatherings, the county cannot solve that for you. That’s the entry point for private professional service.

Types of Professional Mosquito Treatments Available in South Florida

Barrier Spray Treatments: A technician applies a residual product to the foliage, vegetation, and resting sites around the property perimeter. Adult mosquitoes contact treated surfaces when they rest in shade during the day. Effects typically last two to three weeks before the next application cycle. In South Florida’s wet season, rain and humidity can shorten residual effectiveness, so product selection and application timing matter — not every product formulated for a drier climate holds up well here.

Insect Growth Regulators (IGRs): Applied to standing water or combined with barrier sprays, IGRs prevent mosquito larvae from developing into biting adults. They’re a critical complement to adult knockdown because they address the population before it reaches the biting stage. For properties with ornamental ponds, water features, or containers that can’t be fully eliminated, IGR treatment is part of any responsible program.

Larviciding: Direct treatment of standing water sources with biological larvicides (such as Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, known as Bti) or EPA-registered larval control products. Targeting breeding sites directly is one of the most effective long-term population management tools available. Eliminating a breeding site removes the next generation, not just today’s adults.

Station-Based Eco Premium Service: This approach uses strategically placed treatment stations around the property that provide ongoing attractant-based or population-reducing coverage between visits. The Eco Premium program at NaturePest Holistic Pest Control combines station placement with scheduled service visits, creating a layered approach that maintains pressure on the population between technician appointments.

Automated Misting Systems: Timed release systems installed around the property perimeter that dispense product on a programmed schedule. Useful for properties with consistent outdoor entertainment needs — pool decks, outdoor kitchens, waterfront docks. The trade-off is that automated systems release product on a schedule rather than in response to actual population conditions, which can mean unnecessary applications during dry season or insufficient coverage during storm-surge periods. They work best when managed with periodic professional calibration.

Mosquito Bait (ATSB Protocol): Attractive Targeted Sugar Bait (ATSB) is an approach where mosquitoes are drawn to a bait station and ingest a low-dose active ingredient. Because it targets the mosquito’s feeding behavior rather than broadcasting a residual product, the ATSB protocol significantly limits non-target exposure — particularly relevant for properties where pollinators are a concern or where sensitive ecosystems are nearby.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Approach: The most effective programs don’t rely on a single method. IPM combines source reduction (eliminating breeding sites), larviciding, targeted adult control, and population monitoring to manage mosquito pressure with the lowest necessary chemical input. At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, our programs are built on IPM principles — meaning we look at what’s driving population pressure on a specific property before deciding which methods to apply.

Mosquito Control for South Florida’s Unique Property Types

Canal-Front and Waterfront Properties

This is where honest expectation-setting matters most. If your property backs up to a Miami-Dade or Broward canal, you are adjacent to a permanent, continuous mosquito breeding source. The canal system serves as both a drainage network and a Culex quinquefasciatus production zone.

Professional mosquito control on a canal-front property will significantly reduce the population pressure in your immediate yard and outdoor living spaces. What it cannot do is eliminate the source. The canal itself is managed by the South Florida Water Management District and the county — not by your private pest control provider.

The practical approach for canal-adjacent homeowners: treat the property’s vegetation and resting sites aggressively with barrier spray and IGR, apply larvicide to any standing water on the private property side, and use on-demand repellency options (like misting systems or ATSB stations) for high-use outdoor areas. Expect ongoing management to be necessary rather than a one-time fix — this is simply the reality of living near a continuous breeding source, and any provider who tells you otherwise isn’t giving you an accurate picture.

Properties Near Everglades-Adjacent Buffer Zones

Homestead, Kendall, South Miami-Dade, and western Broward areas near the Everglades Agricultural Area sit at the edge of one of the largest wetland ecosystems in North America. Treatment strategies here must account for the fact that you’re managing mosquito pressure that regenerates from adjacent habitat your treatment cannot reach.

In these areas, eco-friendly, low-impact methods take on added weight. Products that could affect non-target aquatic organisms or native wildlife need to be applied with precision — not broadcast. Timing applications away from dawn and dusk, when pollinators and native wildlife are most active, reduces non-target exposure. The University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) Extension program provides research-based guidance for managing pests in environments where proximity to protected ecosystems matters.

HOA Communities and Gated Neighborhoods

South Florida’s density of HOA-governed communities creates a specific challenge: shared spaces like retention ponds, community landscaping, and common-area drainage features may be significant breeding sites that sit outside any individual homeowner’s control.

If your HOA manages community landscaping, you can treat your own yard effectively but still experience significant pressure from untreated common areas. The practical path:

  • Document the community mosquito issue with photos and reports to the HOA management company

  • Request that the HOA contract a licensed provider for common-area treatment, specifically focusing on retention ponds and drainage features

  • Coordinate timing so individual property treatments and community treatments aren’t working against each other

  • As an individual homeowner, focus your private treatment budget on the property envelope immediately surrounding your home and outdoor living spaces

Some HOAs in Miami-Dade and Broward have established community-wide mosquito programs through single-provider contracts — this is the most cost-effective approach and produces noticeably better results than individual homeowners treating in isolation.

Pools, Pool Decks, and Outdoor Entertainment Spaces

South Florida outdoor living culture — pool decks, outdoor kitchens, waterfront docks, rooftop terraces — means mosquito control isn’t just about yard comfort. It’s about whether you can actually use the spaces you’ve invested in.

A properly maintained pool itself isn’t typically a breeding site (chlorination and circulation prevent this). The risks are:

  • Pool covers that collect rainwater

  • Decorative fountains or water features with inadequate circulation

  • Planters and patio furniture that hold water after rain

  • Dense tropical landscaping adjacent to the deck that provides daytime resting habitat for adult mosquitoes

For high-use outdoor spaces, barrier spray timing matters. Applications performed several hours before an outdoor event give the product time to settle and become effective before guests arrive. Misting systems timed for the early evening provide coverage during the highest-pressure activity window for Culex species.

Vacation Rentals and Short-Term Rental Properties

A single mosquito complaint in an Airbnb review can damage a property’s rating in ways that take months to recover. For short-term rental hosts in Miami Beach, Coconut Grove, Fort Lauderdale, or anywhere along the Broward coast, mosquito control isn’t optional — it’s part of the guest experience guarantee.

Recurring professional programs work better for rental properties than one-time treatments because the property turns over constantly, often with outdoor furniture, containers, and landscaping that guests interact with in unpredictable ways. A standing program also gives hosts documentation of active pest management — useful for responding to any complaints and demonstrating due diligence.

From a liability standpoint, a property host in a region with active Dengue and Zika transmission risk has a reasonable duty to maintain the outdoor environment. Active professional mosquito management is part of that standard.

What Happens Over the First Three Treatment Cycles

This is where honest expectation-setting distinguishes good providers from ones who leave customers disappointed.

After the first treatment: You’ll see a noticeable reduction in adult mosquito activity within 24 to 48 hours in treated areas. Adult knockdown from barrier spray application is typically visible within the first day. What this doesn’t address is the larval population already developing in standing water, which will produce new adults within the week. The first treatment establishes a baseline, not a final result.

After the second treatment (typically 3 to 4 weeks later): Population pressure is lower going into this treatment than it was going into the first, because the previous cycle reduced the breeding-to-adult pipeline. Combining adult treatment with larvicide applications begins to interrupt the reproductive cycle. Customers typically notice a more sustained reduction in biting pressure between this treatment and the next.

After the third and fourth treatments: Cumulative population reduction becomes evident. The breeding cycle has been interrupted across multiple generations, and the total population that survived to breed is smaller than what existed before the program started. This is why recurring programs produce meaningfully better results than individual treatments — the effect compounds over time.

Realistic outcome language: Expect significant reduction in biting pressure, not elimination. For properties near canals or Everglades-adjacent areas, some baseline population will persist regardless of treatment frequency because the source is continuous. The goal of a managed recurring program is to keep that baseline at a tolerable level and prevent the explosive seasonal peaks that make outdoor spaces unusable.

How to Vet a Mosquito Control Company in Miami-Dade or Broward

Florida requires pest control operators to be licensed through the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS). Any company applying pesticides to your property — including mosquito treatments — must hold a valid Commercial Pest Control Certificate and each technician must hold a valid Identification Card under the licensee’s Certificate.

Before hiring, verify:

  • Ask for the company’s FDACS Pest Control Certificate number; you can verify active licenses through FDACS directly

  • Confirm the company carries general liability insurance and workers’ compensation coverage

  • Ask specifically which products they use and how they’re applied — a reputable company will answer this question directly

  • Ask about their re-treatment policy if mosquito pressure returns before the next scheduled visit

  • Get any satisfaction guarantee in writing, including what triggers a free re-service

Questions worth asking during the initial assessment:

  1. Do you conduct a property inspection before recommending a program, or is pricing based on square footage alone?

  2. How do your treatments account for South Florida’s wet season and storm events?

  3. What larvicide products do you use, and are they appropriate for use near water features?

  4. How do you handle applications near pollinators and sensitive landscaping?

  5. What’s your approach for properties near canals or wetland buffers?

Red flags to avoid:

  • Companies that quote a price without walking the property

  • One-size-fits-all program pricing with no adjustment for property type or location

  • No written guarantee or service agreement

  • Inability to name the specific products being applied

  • Pressure to commit to an annual contract before any trial service

DIY Mosquito Prevention: What Works Between Professional Treatments

DIY prevention is a meaningful part of any effective program — but it works best as a supplement to professional treatment, not a replacement for it. Here’s what actually makes a difference in South Florida specifically:

Source reduction priorities unique to South Florida:

  • Bromeliads: This one matters more here than almost anywhere in the country. Bromeliads are extremely common in South Florida landscaping and naturally collect water in their leaf axils — a perfect Aedes albopictus breeding site. If you have a bromeliad garden, treat the water-collecting cups with an EPA-registered larvicide tablet (Bti-based products are available at most garden centers) or flush them weekly.

  • Plant saucers: Any container under a potted plant holding standing water is a breeding site. Eliminate them or empty them every few days.

  • Pool covers: Tarped or covered pools that accumulate rainwater are significant breeding sources. Drain accumulated water immediately after rain events.

  • Gutters: Clogged gutters holding decomposing leaf matter and water are ideal Culex breeding habitat. Keep them clear through the wet season.

  • Tarps and outdoor equipment covers: Any surface that cups water after rainfall. Inspect after every rain event.

Landscaping considerations:

Dense tropical plantings — which define South Florida landscaping — provide resting habitat for adult mosquitoes during the day. Trimming vegetation away from the house and thinning dense ground cover near high-use areas reduces daytime harborage. This doesn’t mean eliminating your landscaping; it means managing the density closest to where people spend time.

Personal protection during peak hours:

Aedes aegypti bites primarily during morning and late afternoon. Culex quinquefasciatus is active at night. If you’re working in the yard during these windows without active treatment coverage in place, EPA-registered repellents (DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus) provide meaningful personal protection.

The honest limitation: South Florida’s breeding pressure — particularly during the wet season and after storm events — is high enough that source reduction and personal protection alone will not deliver the reduction most homeowners want from their outdoor spaces. Professional treatment is the layer that handles the adult population and the breeding sites you can’t reach or eliminate.

What to Budget for Mosquito Control in Miami-Dade and Broward

Mosquito control pricing in South Florida varies based on several factors specific to this region:

Property size and type: A compact suburban lot in Pembroke Pines requires a different scope of work than a canal-front acre in Southwest Ranches or a vacation rental condo in Brickell with a shared outdoor terrace.

Treatment method: Station-based programs (like NaturePest’s Eco Premium service), barrier spray programs, and misting system installation each carry different cost structures. Installation of a permanent misting system has an upfront capital cost separate from the ongoing service fees.

Service frequency: Monthly recurring programs deliver cumulative population reduction. Quarterly or bi-monthly programs may be adequate for some properties during dry season months but typically aren’t sufficient through wet season peak pressure.

Proximity to water: Canal-adjacent and Everglades-buffer properties generally require more frequent service to manage ongoing pressure from adjacent breeding sources — expect this to be reflected in program pricing.

What recurring programs typically include vs. what may be add-on:

  • Included: scheduled barrier spray applications, re-service calls between visits if pressure returns

  • May be add-on: larviciding of specific ornamental water features, misting system maintenance, special treatments following tropical weather events

Comparing public free services against private programs: County mosquito control is effectively subsidized by your tax base and covers public infrastructure. It doesn’t cover your property. The value comparison isn’t county service versus private service — it’s the county handling its scope and you handling yours. Both have a role.

Treatment Safety for Children, Pets, and South Florida’s Native Ecosystem

This is a priority concern for health-conscious families in South Florida — and it’s one that deserves a direct, specific answer rather than reassuring generalities.

For children and pets: At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, our mosquito programs are designed as pet-safe and family-friendly applications. Barrier spray treatments are applied to foliage and vegetation; we do not broadcast product on lawn surfaces where children play or pets rest. We allow treated areas to dry fully before re-entry. IGR applications to standing water use Bti-based biologicals or EPA-registered larval control products that target mosquito larvae specifically without the broad-spectrum activity of contact insecticides.

The ATSB protocol, in particular, represents a meaningful advance in this area. Because it works through ingestion by mosquitoes drawn to a bait station rather than through environmental residue, non-target exposure — to pets, children, and beneficial insects — is substantially lower than with traditional broadcast applications.

For pollinators and native ecosystems: South Florida’s biodiversity context makes this a real consideration, particularly for properties near Everglades buffer zones, Crandon Park, Matheson Hammock, or Biscayne Bay’s coastal interface.

Professional-grade targeted applications differ meaningfully from broadcast spraying in a few specific ways:

  • Applications are timed to avoid early morning and late afternoon hours when pollinators (bees, native wasps, butterflies) are most actively foraging

  • Products are applied to resting vegetation rather than to flowering plants

  • Bti-based larvicides are specific to mosquito and black fly larvae and do not affect aquatic invertebrates, fish, or other non-target organisms at standard application rates

This is what no indoor sprays as a core operating principle means in the mosquito context as well — precision application directed at where mosquitoes actually live and breed, rather than treating every surface as a potential problem.

Frequently Asked Questions About Mosquito Control in Miami-Dade and Broward

Is mosquito control safe for children and pets in South Florida?

When applied by a licensed professional using targeted methods, mosquito treatments are safe for households with children and pets. At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, we use pet-safe application protocols — barrier sprays applied to foliage rather than ground surfaces, IGR treatments using biological larvicides where appropriate, and ATSB-based options that significantly reduce non-target exposure. The key is allowing treated surfaces to dry before re-entry, which typically takes 30 to 60 minutes depending on humidity. Ask your provider specifically which products they use and how long to keep children and pets away from treated areas.

How often do I need treatments in Miami-Dade or Broward?

During the wet season (May through October), monthly treatments are the minimum effective frequency for most South Florida properties. After significant storm events, an additional service visit within seven to ten days is often warranted because new breeding populations can reach biting age within a week. During the dry season, some properties can extend to every six to eight weeks. Canal-adjacent and Everglades-buffer properties typically need more frequent service year-round due to continuous breeding pressure from adjacent water sources.

Will my treatment work if my neighbor doesn’t treat their property?

This is a fair question, and the honest answer is: partially. Adult mosquitoes don’t stay stationary — they will move onto your property from adjacent untreated areas. What your treatment does is maintain lower population pressure within your treated space, so that the number of biting mosquitoes you encounter is significantly reduced even if the broader neighborhood population isn’t fully managed. This is also why HOA communities achieve better outcomes when treatment is coordinated across multiple properties rather than handled property-by-property.

What happens to my mosquito service during hurricane season?

Hurricane season and peak mosquito season overlap exactly — June through November. Following a named storm, the population can rebuild rapidly from standing water created by storm surge and flooding. A reliable mosquito control provider should have a protocol for post-storm service visits. At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, we schedule follow-up treatments after significant weather events to address the surge in breeding conditions. When scheduling your program, ask specifically how the company handles post-storm service and whether emergency visits are included in the program fee or billed separately.

Can mosquito control also help with no-see-ums and biting gnats?

No-see-ums (Culicoides species) are common in South Florida coastal areas — Miami Beach, the Brickell waterfront, Coconut Grove marina areas, and anywhere near tidal flats or mangrove edges. They’re not mosquitoes, and they respond differently to treatment. Some barrier spray products provide incidental control of no-see-ums, but targeted management requires a different approach focused on their specific breeding habitat (wet organic soils, mangrove margins). If no-see-ums are part of your problem, mention this during your initial assessment so the program accounts for both species.

How do I report a mosquito problem to Miami-Dade or Broward County?

In Miami-Dade, contact 311 by phone or through the MyMiami311 app to submit a mosquito service request. The county dispatches ground or aerial treatment based on surveillance data and complaint volume. In Broward, service requests can be submitted through Broward County’s online complaint portal. Both systems are most effective for public-space problems — drainage ditches, rights-of-way, and public parks. For mosquito pressure on private property, county services don’t apply and a private licensed provider is the appropriate path.

Do you treat properties near Everglades buffer zones differently?

Yes, and this is a question worth asking any provider you’re considering. Properties near the Everglades-adjacent areas of South Miami-Dade and western Broward require more careful product selection and application to avoid runoff into sensitive freshwater ecosystems. At NaturePest Holistic Pest Control, our approach in these areas uses eco-friendly, targeted methods — Bti-based larvicides, precision adult control, and ATSB protocols — that minimize non-target exposure to native wildlife and aquatic organisms. The goal is effective mosquito reduction that doesn’t create downstream problems in one of North America’s most ecologically significant wetlands.

About NaturePest Holistic Pest Control

NaturePest Holistic Pest Control operates out of Homestead, FL — at 4140 NE 24th St — and serves residential and commercial properties throughout Miami-Dade and Broward counties. Miami-Dade County collected 399,418 Aedes aegypti mosquitoes PLOS ONE (2026), and 1,250,879 Culex quinquefasciatus mosquitoes PLOS ONE (2026), using 308 mosquito traps for eight years of surveillance PLOS ONE (2026). Our mosquito control programs include targeted barrier spray with IGR, station-based Eco Premium service, breeding-site treatment, mosquito bait using the ATSB protocol, automated misting options, and on-demand repellency applications.

All programs are built on Integrated Pest Management principles: assess the specific property first, identify the driving species and breeding sources, select treatment methods appropriate to those conditions, and schedule follow-up based on the property’s actual needs rather than a standard calendar. Our approach uses fewer chemical applications than conventional mosquito programs, and our no indoor sprays policy extends to our mosquito work — we don’t treat interior spaces as a matter of standard practice.

NaturePest Holistic Pest Control is rated 4.9 out of 178 NaturePest Holistic Pest Control reviews. We hold all required FDACS pest control certifications and back our programs with a 100% pest-free satisfaction guarantee.

For a property assessment and program recommendation, contact us at (786) 222-7069 (Monday through Friday 8 AM to 6 PM, Saturday 8 AM to 12 PM) or visit naturepest.com to learn more about our mosquito programs for Miami-Dade and Broward properties.
